lines: Finding the right work is harder when everyone asks if you found it yet.
Work is work. Finding the right work is the tricky part.
Waiting for work is still work if you look <pulse>worried enough</pulse>.
Where do I fit? Somewhere useful, I hope, preferably before supper.
People with trades get tasks. People without trades get errands.
A fair chance is easier to ask for than to recognize.
Most days, I am at the village square, trying to find a calling before everyone else makes it their business.
People think watching is simple until something goes wrong and suddenly it is very important.
A village runs on small work. Nobody praises it until it stops happening.
I trust empty hands more than a loud promise. At least they are honest.
A free pair of hands can be useful if someone knows where to point them.
Work sounds simple until it has to fit the day in front of you.
I notice job sites the way hungry people notice bread.
Not having a trade does not mean not having eyes.
A village always has work. The trick is finding the kind that wants you back.
I have learned a little from everyone and enough to be dangerous with none of it.
Useful people ask where the need is before bragging about skill.
Some days I am between callings. Some days the callings are avoiding me.
A good opportunity looks a lot like a chore until it pays off.
I keep my hands ready because waiting empty feels worse.
Trades choose people strangely. I am keeping myself available.
You learn plenty by watching masters avoid simple mistakes.
I may not have a station, but I know when the square feels wrong.
There is dignity in being ready before anyone asks.
A village needs spare help more often than it admits.
I am trying to look useful, not involved.
Keep your voice even. I am listening for what you leave out.
Some questions are safer when they stand a little farther away.
Did someone ask you to move those supplies, or did you decide on your own?
I can help, but I need to know what we are walking into first.
Why is everyone near the well pretending not to watch the road?
If that job is harmless, why has nobody else taken it?
I keep a free hand in case the village needs help quickly.
Do you know who left the gate unlatched last night?
I would rather ask one awkward question than clean up one bad surprise.
Is there a reason the square went quiet when you arrived?
I can carry the crate. You can explain why it is humming.
Nobody assigned me to watch the lane, but somebody should.
Are you offering work, or trying to get me away from the village?
I have no trade to protect, so I notice when people avoid giving details.
Tell me where the task is before you tell me how easy it will be.
I am willing to help. I am not willing to guess what the danger is.
Did the bell ring once, or did I imagine it?
I know how this sounds, but that cart was not there this morning.
If we are going beyond the fields, I want someone to know where we went.
I followed you once and learned something. I need better shoes before I choose a trade.
I remember following you down that road. My feet remember it even better.
Why did you choose the rough path when the lower road looked clear?
Did you know our food would run short before we saw the village again?
How did you keep track of every turn once the light started fading?
Were you worried when the bell disappeared behind the hill?
What made you trust that bridge after we saw the missing boards?
Did you notice I was falling behind before I said anything?
How close were we to taking the wrong fork by the old tree?
Was the detour safer, or did it only feel safer because it was quiet?
Why did the road seem longer after we used the last of the bread?
Did you hear something following us near the stone wall?
What would you pack differently if we walked that route again?
How did you know the lights ahead belonged to our village?
Were you as relieved as I was when the gate finally came into view?
Did sharing the last meal bother you, or were you too tired to care?
What kept you moving when the ground turned steep?
Would you take the same road home if we made that trip again?
Did you plan every stop, or were you choosing as we went?
Next time we travel that far, can we agree to rest before my feet go numb?
I followed you into a boat once. Not a trade, apparently, but it felt like training.
That boat trip still sits strangely with me. How did you stay so calm?
Did you know the current would pull that hard before we left shore?
When the village vanished behind us, were you worried too?
What made you trust that little boat with both of us?
Did you hear the water knocking against the hull all the way home?
How close were we to tipping when I shifted my weight?
Was sitting still really the most useful thing I could do?
Did you plan where we would land, or did the current decide for us?
What would you pack differently if we made that trip again?
Were you watching the shoreline while I watched the water?
Did the boat feel that cramped to you, or was that just me?
Which mistake rocked us worst? I remember making several.
How long did it take you to feel steady after we stepped onto land?
Would a second paddle have helped, or only given me something else to drop?
Did you ever doubt we would see the village again?
What was that sound under the boat when we crossed the deep water?
Why did nobody warn me that a quiet trip could feel so tense?
Did you choose that route because it was safe or because it was quick?
If we go by boat again, can I sit in the middle this time?
